552.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable of the word ('recai sempre sobre a última sílaba'); compounds and derived stems re-stress so that the final syllable of the whole form carries the primary (e.g. /maraka"ja/ + /"ʔɨ/ → [maɾaˌkadʒa"ʔɨ] 'gato do mato').
552.srule: In words of three or more syllables the odd-numbered syllables counted from the right (3rd, 5th... from the end) also carry an intensity peak: secondary stress alternates leftward from the final primary stress, e.g. [jaˌhitaˈtã] 'estrela', [taˌmanũˈhã] 'tamanduá', [ˌpaoˈho] 'mão grande', [maɾaˌkadʒaˈʔɨ] 'gato do mato'.

tn.quote: Itunyoso Trique has nine contrastive tones: four level tones, three falling tones, and two rising tones. All tones contrast in root-final syllables, but only three level tones contrast in penultimate syllables and two in antepenults. Any level or falling tone may surface on final open syllables, whereas the rising tones surface only in final syllables with the coda /h/. All level tones and two of the falling tones also surface in this environment. Only level tones may surface preceding a glottal stop coda.

qtr.text: As in almost all Bantu languages, the tonic accent in Subiya falls on the penultimate. Ex.: mu-kwáme, man; izúba, sun, etc. Monosyllables are either proclitic or enclitic, i.e. as far as the accent is concerned they must be regarded as forming one unit with the words they precede or follow. Ex.: mwan'á ngu, my child; a bá di ku chíta, he was doing, etc. Some monosyllabic verbs do however carry the accent; thus: ba í, they went; ba sí, they dug, ba dí, they ate, etc. Others do not, thus bá ti: they said, etc.

560.dq: Kĩsêdjê's lexicon contains stressed and unstressed items, the latter being the particles I have been calling clitics. Stress is iambic, with main stress falling on the last underlying syllable of stressed words (158). Clitics are phrased together with a neighboring stressed word but, as exemplified by (159), don't bear either primary or secondary stress.

561.quote: Content words contain at least two vowels. Some functors, such as the conjunction ma ‘and’, are monosyllabic. Stress falls on the penultimate vowel of a word with secondary stress assigned to every second syllable to the left. All vowel sequences occur with the exception of /uo/. This includes double vowels (sequences of two identical vowels) /ii/, /ee/, /aa/, /oo/ and /uu/. Such double vowels are realised phonetically as a single long vowel, i.e. [iː], [ɛː], [aː], [ɔː] and [uː]. Given the placement of stress, one member of a vowel sequence will always bear stress.

evidence_works.work: Tamelan 2021, A grammar of Dela: an Austronesian language of Rote, eastern Indonesia (PhD thesis, The Australian National University: pp. 36-38, sec. 2.2.5-2.2.5.1)
evidence_works.detail: For Dela: 'Word stress in Dela falls on the penultimate syllable of the root. Since each vowel is a syllable nucleus, it is the penultimate segmental vowel that carries the stress. Roots with two metrical feet have secondary stress on the initial syllable.... Affixes, partial reduplication, enclitics (including sentence/phrasal enclitics) and paragogic vowels are extrametrical, which means they are not counted in stress assignment, and stress does not shift.' (p. 36); 'the secondary stress in quadrisyllabic roots and trisyllabic words that are formed from the deletion of the antepenultimate syllable falls on the initial syllable of the roots (or on every second syllable preceding the primary stress-bearing syllable)' (p. 38); 'trisyllabic and quadrisyllabic affixed and reduplicated words do not have secondary stresses' (p. 38). This agrees with the entry's penultimate primary stress and every-second-syllable secondary stress for roots, and adds the qualification, for Dela only, that the domain is the root with affixes, reduplicants, enclitics and paragogic vowels extrametrical, so that affixed and reduplicated words carry no secondary stress.

In their original study of tone in East Kewa (Kewapi) the Franklins ... establish two contrasting level tones: a high tone and a low tone, and four word tone patterns, High (H), Low (L), High Low (HL) and Low High (LH). ... 576.quote: Syllable structure can be open - CV (e.g. ka+ju ‘steel.axe’); or closed - CVC (e.g. ngam+purr ‘care’) or, less commonly, CVCC (e.g. tarrp ‘gone forever’). Consonant clusters are examined in §2.2.3. Primary stress falls on the first syllable of a word.
